# Lecture 6: Continuous distributions and the normal model {#b06} ::: {.outcomes} By the end of Lecture 6, you can - distinguish a continuous random variable from a discrete one; - explain why $P(X=x)=0$ for a continuous random variable and interpret a probability density function as area rather than point probability; - use a CDF to calculate interval probabilities; - calculate uniform probabilities from interval lengths; - standardise a normal value and compute normal probabilities by hand from supplied $Z$ values and with `pnorm()`; - convert a percentile back to a raw value with $x=\mu+z\sigma$ and verify with `qnorm()`; - find quantiles of model distributions (the uniform median, normal quartiles); - check a proposed normal model against a histogram of data and say when it fails. ::: ::: {.driving-question} Driving question

Not everything comes in whole numbers: negotiation time, invested amounts, and revenues can land anywhere in a range. Insurers, lenders, and operations planners price risk on exactly such quantities every day --- and that needs a new kind of probability model.

Negotiation time and invested amounts can take any value in a range. How do we assign probabilities when no single value has any? ::: ::: {.course-phase .phase-before} ## Before class Total preparation time: about 30 minutes.
Video preparation (20 minutes)
Watch Probability Density Functions, Uniform Random Variables, and Normal Random Variables. Focus on the difference between density height and probability, and on the roles of the two normal parameters. All links are also listed in the External Video Guide.
**Reactivate (5 minutes).** A discrete random variable has separated possible values (Lecture 3 attached a PMF and a CDF to such variables). A continuous random variable can take every real value in an interval. Match each variable to the better description: 1. number of sharks in an on-air deal; 2. exact time spent negotiating a pitch; 3. season number; 4. exact amount invested, before rounding to dollars. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answers Variables 1 and 3 are discrete. Variables 2 and 4 are continuous in a mathematical model, even if a measuring device or database records rounded values. ::: **Predict (5 minutes).** Answer the one-click Mentimeter question posted on Canvas before you come to class: for a *continuous* random variable $X$, is $P(X = \text{exactly } 10)$ **very small** or **exactly zero**? Commit to an answer; the lecture resolves it. If powers, square roots, inequalities, or z-score algebra feel unfamiliar, review [Mathematics Refresher: powers, functions, and intervals](../resources/math-refresher.html). ::: ::: {.course-phase .phase-in-class} ## In class The session opens with the usual four-minute entry quiz on the prep videos, then turns to the driving question. Start with the prediction from your prep. For a continuous random variable, $$P(X=x)=0 \quad\text{for every single value } x.$$ Not very small --- exactly zero. An interval contains infinitely many values; if each single value carried even the tiniest positive probability, the total would exceed 1. Yet the negotiation certainly takes *some* amount of time, so probability has not disappeared. It has moved: probability now belongs to **intervals**, not points. That forces a new object to replace the PMF, and building that object is the first job of this lecture. ### From probability mass to probability density

MIT explanation (review): 08.2 Probability Density Functions.

For a discrete random variable, the PMF assigns probability to individual values. For a continuous random variable $X$, a **probability density function** (PDF), written $f_X(x)$, is a non-negative curve whose total area is 1. The probability that $X$ lies between $a$ and $b$ is the **area** under the curve between those values. You do not need calculus in this course. You need to interpret probability as area and use a CDF, R, or supplied values to calculate it. The crucial reading rule: **density is height, probability is area.** Density is probability *per unit* of $x$ --- roughly, the probability of a tiny interval divided by its width. Because a width can be small, the height can be large. A density can exceed 1 as long as the total area under the curve is 1. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check: is a rectangle of width 0.5 and height 2 a valid density? Yes. The curve is non-negative and its total area is $0.5 \times 2 = 1$, so it is a legitimate PDF (a uniform density on an interval of length 0.5). The height 2 is not a probability --- no probability statement here exceeds 1, because every probability is an area inside that rectangle. Height 2 simply means the probability is packed into a narrow range. ::: #### The CDF works for every random variable The cumulative distribution function is still $$F_X(x)=P(X\le x),$$ exactly as in Lecture 3. For a continuous random variable, $$P(aMIT explanation (review): 05.5 Uniform Random Variables.

If every equal-length subinterval of $[a,b]$ is equally likely, then $X\sim U(a,b)$. Its density is constant: $$f_X(x)=\frac{1}{b-a},\qquad a\le x\le b,$$ and zero outside the **support** $[a,b]$. The height is not a choice --- it is *forced* by the requirement that the whole rectangle have area 1: $$\text{width}\times\text{height}=(b-a)\times\frac{1}{b-a}=1.$$ Because the height is constant, interval probability depends only on interval length. For $a\le cMIT explanation (review): 08.8 Normal Random Variables.

A normal random variable is written $$X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2).$$ Read the notation carefully: the second parameter is the **variance** $\sigma^2$, not the standard deviation. The density is symmetric and bell-shaped. The parameter $\mu$ locates its centre; $\sigma>0$ controls its spread: $$E[X]=\mu,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(X)=\sigma^2.$$ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="See the R code for this figure"} library(ggplot2) normal_curve <- data.frame(z = seq(-3.6, 3.6, length.out = 800)) normal_curve$density <- dnorm(normal_curve$z) ggplot(normal_curve, aes(z, density)) + geom_area(data = subset(normal_curve, z >= -1 & z <= 1), fill = "#009E73", alpha = 0.25) + geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1, 1), linetype = "dashed", colour = "#5B6976", linewidth = 0.5) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#C98B2E", linewidth = 0.7) + geom_line(colour = "#17324D", linewidth = 1.2) + annotate("text", x = 0, y = 0.16, label = "about 68%", colour = "#17324D", size = 3.4) + annotate("text", x = 0.15, y = 0.425, label = "mean~mu", parse = TRUE, colour = "#17324D", size = 3.4, hjust = 0) + scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(-2, -1, 0, 1, 2), labels = expression(mu - 2 * sigma, mu - sigma, mu, mu + sigma, mu + 2 * sigma)) + scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 0.43), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.02))) + labs(x = "Value of X", y = "Density") + theme_minimal(base_size = 13) + theme( panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(), plot.caption = element_text(colour = "#5B6976"), axis.title = element_text(colour = "#17324D") ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The normal density. The shaded central area between the two grey dashed lines runs from one standard deviation below the mean to one above and contains about 68% of the distribution; the gold dashed line marks the mean μ.](b06-continuous-normal_files/figure-html/fig-b06-normal-shape-1.png){#fig-b06-normal-shape width=672} ::: ::: The horizontal axis locates possible values relative to $\mu$ and $\sigma$; the vertical axis is density, and probability is again area. In the normal **model**, about 68% of the distribution lies within one standard deviation of the mean and about 95% within 1.96 standard deviations. These are facts about the mathematical model --- the caveat box below explains why they are not automatic facts about every dataset. #### Standardising: every normal question becomes a Z question If $X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)$, then $$Z=\frac{X-\mu}{\sigma}\sim N(0,1).$$ A z-score reports how many standard deviations a value lies above or below the mean. Standardising matters because the closed-book exam supplies a handful of standard-normal probabilities on the page --- your job is to translate the business question into a $Z$ question that those supplied values can answer. The hand calculation is the primary route; R only verifies it. ::: {#exm-b06-supplied-z} ## Worked example: normal probabilities from supplied Z values Processing time $Y$ (in minutes) is modelled as $Y\sim N(50,100)$. The 68% and 95% rules are exact statements about the mathematical normal model; quoting them for a variable that is skewed, bounded, or spiked (most business variables are at least one of these) produces confident-sounding numbers that are simply wrong. Model probabilities such as $P(Y\le 65)=0.9332$ are conclusions *inside* the model $N(50,100)$; they say nothing about reality unless the model describes the data. And a fitted curve that matches the mean and SD of the data can still miss the shape entirely --- matching two summaries is not a fit. The legitimate uses ahead: the normal as a checked model for some variables, and --- from Lecture 8 --- as the reliable model for sampling distributions of averages, where mathematics rather than wishful thinking puts it there. ::: ### Answering the driving question No single negotiation time or invested amount has positive probability --- $P(X=x)=0$ --- so probabilities are assigned to **intervals** as areas under a density.
